nodes.statement_short: Adapt the grid interpretation formulas with wrap-around clauses at the frame boundary so that an $m\times k$ frame interprets an $m\times k$ torus.

nodes.name: Pi^0_1-hardness with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement: Let $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $\beta$ be the corresponding betweenness relation. Assume that $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$. The first-order theory of the class $\{(T,\beta,P)\mid P\subseteq T\text{ is finite}\}$ is $\Pi^0_1$-hard.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
assumptions: Let $T\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $\beta$ be the corresponding betweenness relation.
Assume that $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$.
conclusions: The first-order theory of the class $\{(T,\beta,P)\mid P\subseteq T\text{ is finite}\}$ is $\Pi^0_1$-hard.

nodes.name: Proof of Pi^0_1-hardness with a finite predicate
nodes.statement: Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $n\geq 2$. Let $\sigma=\{H,V\}$ be the vocabulary of tori, and let $\tau=\{\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$ be the vocabulary of labelled finite Cartesian frames. By Lemma \ref{finitedefinable}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem with a first-order $\tau$-sentence that defines the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$. Let $\varphi^S_{\mathit{fCf}}$ denote such a sentence. By Lemma \ref{torusinterpretablelemma}, there is a computable function $J$ such that for all inputs $S$ to the periodic tiling problem, the function $J$ is a uniform interpretation of the class of $S$-labelled tori in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with domain $T$. By Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem with a first-order $\sigma\cup S$-sentence $\varphi_S$ such that for all tori $\mathfrak{B}$, the torus $\mathfrak{B}$ is $S$-tilable iff there is an expansion $\mathfrak{B}^*$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^*\models\varphi_{S}$. Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of tile symbols. Define the first-order $\tau$-sentence \[ \gamma_S:=\varphi_{\mathit{fCf}}^S\wedge J(\varphi_S). \] We will prove that for each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$. \item There exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable. \end{enumerate} Thereby we establish that there exists a computable reduction from the complement problem of the periodic tiling problem to the membership problem of the first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$ with a finite predicate. Since the periodic tiling problem is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete, its complement problem is $\Pi^0_1$-complete. Let $S$ be an input to the periodic tiling problem. First assume that there exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{T}^*$ of $\mathfrak{T}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{T}^*\models \varphi_S$. Since the function $J$ is a uniform interpretation of the class of $S$-labelled tori in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$, and since $\mathfrak{T}^*\models\varphi_S$, it follows by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that there exists an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ with the domain $T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models J(\varphi_S)$. Since $\mathfrak{C}$ is an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame, we have that $\mathfrak{C}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fcf}$. Therefore $\mathfrak{C}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fcf}\wedge J(\varphi_S)$. Hence the finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ is an expansion of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models\gamma_S$. For the converse, assume that there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{B}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fCf}$ and $\mathfrak{B}\models J_S(\varphi_S)$. Since $\mathfrak{B}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fCf}$, the structure $\mathfrak{B}$ is an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame with domain $T$. Therefore, and since $\mathfrak{B}\models J(\varphi_S)$, we conclude by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi_S$ holds for some $S$-labelled torus $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence by Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma} there exists a torus that is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Reduction from the complement of the periodic tiling problem: $\gamma_S=\varphi^S_{fCf}\wedge J(\varphi_S)$ is satisfiable with finite $P$ iff some torus is $S$-tilable.

nodes.name: First part: universal WMSO not in MSO
nodes.statement: It is easy to observe that $\forall\mathrm{WMSO}\not\leq\mathrm{MSO}$: consider the sentence $\forall X\exists y\, \neg Xy$. This $\forall\mathrm{WMSO}$ sentence is true in a model iff the domain of the model is infinite. A straightforward monadic second-order Ehrenfeucht-Fra\"{i}ss\'{e} game argument can be used to establish that infinity is not expressible by any $\mathrm{MSO}$ sentence.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: The $\forall$WMSO sentence $\forall X\exists y\neg Xy$ expresses infinity, which MSO cannot (EF game).

nodes.name: Second part: separating structures
nodes.statement: To show that $\forall\mathrm{MSO}\not\leq\mathrm{WMSO}$, consider the structures $(\mathbb{R},<)$ and $(\mathbb{Q},<)$. The structures can be separated by a sentence of $\forall\mathrm{MSO}$ stating that every subset bounded from above has a least upper bound.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Use $(\mathbb{R},<)$ vs $(\mathbb{Q},<)$, separated by the $\forall$MSO least-upper-bound sentence.

nodes.name: WMSO game variant
nodes.statement: To see that the two structures cannot be separated by any sentence of $\mathrm{WMSO}$, consider the variant of the $\mathrm{MSO}$ Ehrenfeucht-Fra\"{i}ss\'{e} game where the players choose \emph{finite sets} in addition to domain elements. It is easy to establish that this game characterizes the expressivity of $\mathrm{WMSO}$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the EF game with finite sets, characterizing WMSO.

nodes.name: Duplicator strategy
nodes.statement: To see that the duplicator has a winning strategy in a game of any finite length played on the structures $(\mathbb{R},<)$ and $(\mathbb{Q},<)$, we devise an extension of the folklore winning strategy in the corresponding first-order game. Firstly, the duplicator can obviously always pick an element whose betweenness configuration corresponds exactly to that of the element picked by the spoiler. Furthermore, even if the spoiler picks a finite set, it is easy to see that the duplicator can pick his set such that each of its elements respect the betweenness configuration of the set picked by the spoiler.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Duplicator copies betweenness configurations of elements and finite sets, so WMSO cannot separate.

nodes.name: Reduce to closed, bounded, discrete
nodes.statement: We shall first establish that a set $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is finite iff it is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points of $T$. Recall that an isolated point $u$ of a set $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a point such that there exists some open ball $B$ such that $B\cap U =\{u\}$.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: First show finite iff closed, bounded and consisting of isolated points.

nodes.name: Finite implies closed, bounded, discrete
nodes.statement: Assume $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is finite. Since $T$ is finite, we can find a minimum distance between points in the set $T$. Therefore it is clear that each point $t$ in $T$ belongs to some open ball $B$ such that $B\cap T = \{t\}$, and hence $T$ consists of isolated points. Similarly, since $T$ is finite, each point $b$ in the complement of $T$ has some minimum distance to the points of $T$, and therefore $b$ belongs to some open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus T$. Hence the set $T$ is the complement of the union of open balls $B$ such that $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus T$, and therefore $T$ is closed. Finally, since $T$ is finite, we can find a maximum distance between the points in $T$, and therefore $T$ is bounded.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: A finite set has minimal separations and a maximal distance.

nodes.name: Closed, bounded, discrete implies finite
nodes.statement: Assume then that $T\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points of $T$. Since $T$ consists of isolated points, it has an open cover $\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathrm{Pow}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ such that each set in $\mathcal{C}$ contains exactly one point $t\in T$. The set $\mathcal{C}$ is an open cover of $T$, and by the Heine-Borel theorem, there exists a finite subcover $\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$ of the set $T$. Since $\mathcal{D}$ is finite and each set in $\mathcal{D}$ contains exactly one point of $T$, the set $T$ must also be finite.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Apply Heine-Borel to a cover by balls each containing one point.

nodes.name: Plan the FO formula
nodes.statement: We then conclude the proof by establishing that there exists a first-order formula $\varphi(P)$ stating that the unary predicate $P$ is closed, bounded and consists of isolated points.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: It remains to express closed, bounded and discrete in first-order logic.

nodes.name: Define parallel
nodes.statement:
We will first define a formula $\mathit{parallel}(x,y,t,k)$ stating that the lines defined by $x,y$ and $t,k$ are parallel in $(\mathbb{R}^n, eta)$. We define  egin{align*} &\mathit{parallel}(x,y,t,k):= x
eq y\wedge t
eq k \wedge \Big((\mathit{collinear}(x,y,t)\wedge \mathit{collinear}(x,y,k))\ &\quad\vee  ig(
eg\exists z(\mathit{collinear}(x,y,z)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(t,k,z))\ &\quad\quad\wedge \exists z_1 z_2(x
eq z_1\wedge\mathit{collinear}(x,y,z_1)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(x,t,z_2)\wedge\mathit{collinear}(z_1,z_2,k))\,  ig)\Big). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Define the FO formula parallel(x,y,t,k).

nodes.name: Define basis and flat
nodes.statement: We will then define first-order $\{\beta\}$-formulae $\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)$ and $\mathit{flat}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z)$ using simultaneous recursion. The first formula states that the vectors corresponding to the pairs $(x_0,x_i)$, $1\leq i\leq k$, form a basis of a $k$-dimensional flat. The second formula states that the point $z$ is in the span of the basis defined by the vectors $(x_0,x_i)$, the origin being $x_0$. First define $\mathit{basis}_0(x_0):= x_0=x_0$ and $\mathit{flat}_0(x_0,z):= x_0=z$. Then define $\mathit{flat}_k$ and $\mathit{basis_k}$ recursively in the following way. \begin{align*} &\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k):=\mathit{basis}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1})\wedge \neg \mathit{flat}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1},x_k),\\ &\mathit{flat}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z):=\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)\\ &\quad\wedge \exists y_0\dots \exists y_k\Big(y_0=x_0 \wedge y_k=z \wedge\bigwedge_{i\, \leq\, k-1} \big(y_i=y_{i+1}\vee\mathit{parallel}(x_0,x_{i+1},y_i,y_{i+1})\big)\Big). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Define basis_k and flat_k by simultaneous recursion.

nodes.name: Define open triangles
nodes.statement: We then define a first-order $\{\beta,P\}$-formula $\mathit{sepr}(x,P)$ asserting that $x$ belongs to an open ball $B$ such that each point in $B\setminus\{x\}$ belongs to the complement of $P$. The idea is to state that there exist $n+1$ points $x_0,\dots,x_n$ that form an \emph{$n$-dimensional triangle} around $x$, and every point contained in the triangle (with $x$ being a possible exception) belongs to the complement of $P$. Every open ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is contained in some $n$-dimensional triangle in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and vice versa. We will recursively define first-order formulae $\mathit{opentriangle}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k,z)$ stating that $z$ is properly inside a $k$-dimensional triangle defined by $x_0,\dots,x_k$, see Figure \ref{fig:opentriangle}. First define $\mathit{opentriangle}_1(x_0,x_1,z):=\beta^*(x_0,z,x_1)$, and then define \begin{align*} &\mathit{opentriangle}_{k}(x_0,\dots,x_k,z):=\mathit{basis}_k(x_0,\dots,x_k)\\ &\quad\wedge \exists y\big(\mathit{opentriangle}_{k-1}(x_0,\dots,x_{k-1},y)\wedge \beta^*(y,z,x_k)\big). \end{align*} \begin{figure} \centering \includegraphics[scale=2]{finiteness2} \caption{The figure shows how the formula $\mathit{opentriangle}_2(y,z,u,x)$ is interpreted.} \end{figure}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Define opentriangle_k recursively to express open neighbourhoods.

nodes.name: Define sepr
nodes.statement: We are now ready to define $\mathit{sepr}(x,P)$. Let \begin{multline*} \mathit{sepr}(x,P) := \exists x_0\dots \exists x_n\Bigl(\mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots, x_n,x)\\ \wedge \forall y \big((\mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n,y)\wedge y\neq x)\rightarrow \neg Py\big)\Bigr). \end{multline*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: Define sepr(x,P): an open triangle around x avoids P except at x.

nodes.name: Express closed and discrete
nodes.statement: Now, the sentence $\varphi_1:=\forall x\bigl(\neg Px\ \rightarrow\ \mathit{sepr}(x,P)\bigr)$ states that each point in the complement of $P$ is contained in an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P$. The sentence therefore states that the complement of $P$ is a union of open balls. Since the set of unions of open balls is exactly the same as the set of open sets, the sentence states that $P$ is closed. The sentence $\varphi_2:=\forall x\bigl(Px\ \rightarrow\ \mathit{sepr}(x,P)\bigr)$ clearly states that $P$ consists of isolated points.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_1$ says P is closed, $\varphi_2$ that P consists of isolated points.

nodes.name: Express bounded
nodes.statement: Finally, in order to state that $P$ is bounded, we define a formula asserting that there exist points $x_0,\dots,x_n$ that form an n-dimensional triangle around $P$. \begin{multline*} \varphi_3:=\exists x_0\dots \exists x_n\Bigl(\mathit{basis}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n) \wedge \forall y\bigl(Py\rightarrow \mathit{opentriangle}_n(x_0,\dots,x_n,y)\bigr)\Bigr) \end{multline*}
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: $\varphi_3$ says an n-dimensional triangle contains P.

nodes.name: Conclude finiteness is definable
nodes.statement: The conjunction $\varphi_1\wedge\varphi_2\wedge\varphi_3$ states that $P$ is finite.
nodes.section: 3 Expressivity of universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ and weak universal $\mathrm{MSO}$ over affine real structures $(\mathbb{R}^n,\beta)$
nodes.statement_short: The conjunction of the three sentences defines finiteness.

nodes.name: Define sequence(P)
nodes.statement: Define \[ \mathit{sequence}(P):=\exists x\, Px\, \wedge\, \forall x\forall y\forall z\, \bigl(Px\wedge Py \wedge Pz\ \rightarrow\ \mathit{collinear}(x,y,z)\bigr). \] The formula $sequence(P)$ states that $P$ is a sequence.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Write the FO formula sequence(P).

nodes.name: Discretely spaced is FO
nodes.statement: By inspection of Definition \ref{discretelyspaceddfn}, it is easy to see that there is a first-order formula $\psi$ such that the conjunction $sequence(P)\wedge\psi$ states that $P$ is a discretely spaced sequence.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: By inspection, discrete spacing is first-order.

nodes.name: Remaining clauses are FO
nodes.statement: Continuing this trend, it is straightforward to observe that Definitions \ref{discretelyinfinitedfn}, \ref{sequencewithzero} and \ref{omegalikedfn} specify first-order properties, and therefore there exists a first-order formula $\varphi_{\omega}(P)$ stating that $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: The remaining defining conditions are first-order, giving $\varphi_\omega(P)$.

nodes.name: Embedding of N
nodes.statement: We denote by $i_0$ the unique zero-point of $P$. Since $P$ is a discretely infinite sequence, it has a base point. Clearly $i_0$ has to be the only base point of $P$. It is straightforward to establish that since $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence with the base point $i_0$, there exists a sequence $(a_i)_{i\in \mathbb{N}}$ of points $a_i\in P$ such that $i_0=a_0$ and $a_{i+1}$ is the unique $E$-successor of $a_{i}$ for all $i\in \mathbb{N}$. Define the function $h:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow P$ such that $h(i) = a_i$ for all $i\in\mathbb{N}$. It is easy to see that $h$ is an embedding of $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ into $(P,E)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: From the zero-point $i_0$ build the successor chain $a_i$; $h(i)=a_i$ embeds $(\mathbb{N},succ)$ into $(P,E)$.

nodes.name: Case T = R^n
nodes.statement: Assume then that $T=\mathbb{R}^n$. We shall show that the function $h:\mathbb{N}\longrightarrow P$ is a surjection.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: For $T=\mathbb{R}^n$, show $h$ is surjective.

nodes.name: Coordinatise the line
nodes.statement: Let $d$ denote the canonical metric of $\mathbb{R}$, and let $d_R$ be the restriction of the canonical metric of $\mathbb{R}^n$ to the line $R$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $P\subseteq R$. Let $g:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow R$ be the isometry from $(\mathbb{R},d)$ to $(R,d_R)$ such that $g(0) = i_0 = h(0)$ and such that for all $r\in\mathit{ran}(h)$, we have $\beta\bigl(i_0,g(1),r\bigr)$ or $\beta\bigl(i_0,r,g(1)\bigr)$. Let $(R,\leq^R)$ be the structure, where $$\leq^{R}\ =\ \{\ (u,v)\in R\times R\ |\ g^{-1}(u)\, \leq^{\mathbb{R}}\, g^{-1}(v)\ \}.$$
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the isometry $g$ and the induced order $\leq^R$ on the line.

nodes.name: Least upper bound
nodes.statement: If $\mathit{ran}(h)$ is not bounded from above w.r.t. $\leq^R$, then $h$ must be a surjection. Therefore assume that $\mathit{ran}(h)$ is bounded above. By the Dedekind completeness of the reals, there exists a least upper bound $s\in R$ of $\mathit{ran}(h)$ w.r.t. $\leq^R$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: If ran(h) is bounded, take its least upper bound $s$ by Dedekind completeness.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: Notice that since $h$ is an embedding of $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ into $(P,E)$, we have $s\not\in\mathit{ran}(h)$. Due to the definition of $E$, it is sufficient to show that $\{\, t\in P\ |\ s\leq^R t\ \} = \emptyset$ in order to conclude that $h$ maps onto $P$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to show no point of $P$ lies at or beyond $s$.

nodes.name: s not in P
nodes.statement: Assume that the least upper bound $s$ belongs to the set $P$. Since $P$ is a discretely spaced sequence, there is a point $u\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{s\}$ such that $\beta(s,u,i_0)$ and $$\forall r\in\mathbb{R}^n \bigl(\beta^*(s,r,u) \rightarrow r\not\in P\bigl).$$ Now $u<^R s$ and the points $u$ and $s$ are linearly $(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P)$-connected, implying that $s$ cannot be the least upper bound of $\mathit{ran}(h)$. This is a contradiction. Therefore $s\not\in P$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: If $s\in P$, discrete spacing contradicts $s$ being the least upper bound.

nodes.name: No point of P beyond s
nodes.statement: Assume, ad absurdum, that there exists a point $t\in P$ such that $\beta(i_0,s,t)$. Now, since $P$ is an $\omega$-like sequence, there exists points $u',v'\in P\setminus\{s\}$ such that $\beta(u',s,v')$ and $$\forall r\in \mathbb{R}^n\bigl(\beta^*(u',r,v')\rightarrow r\not\in P\bigr).$$ We have $\beta(s,u',i_0)$ or $\beta(s,v',i_0)$. Assume, by symmetry, that $\beta(s,u',i_0)$. Now $u'<^R s$, and the points $u'$ and $s$ are linearly $(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus P)$-connected. Hence, since $s\not\in \mathit{ran}(h)$, we conclude that $s$ is not the least upper bound of $\mathit{ran}(h)$. This is a contradiction.
nodes.section: 4.1 Lines and sequences
nodes.statement_short: A point beyond $s$ contradicts $\omega$-likeness at $s$.

nodes.name: Fix S and frame
nodes.statement: Let $S\not=\emptyset$ be a finite set of tile symbols. Let $\mathfrak{C} = (T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Fix $S$ and an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We shall show how an $S$-labelled supergrid $\mathfrak{G}_{\mathfrak{C}}$ is interpreted in $\mathfrak{C}$. Figures \ref{fig:triangle} and \ref{fig:triangle_tiled} illustrate the related constructions.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Show how a supergrid is interpreted in $\mathfrak{C}$.

nodes.name: Two pencils of lines
nodes.statement: The domain of the interpretation of $\mathfrak{G}_{\mathfrak{C}}$ in $\mathfrak{C}$ will be the set of intersection points of two sets of lines defined as follows. The first set of lines is formed by connecting the point $p_y$ to each of the points $u$ in the set $$\{x\in P\mid \beta(p_0,x,p_x)\}\setminus\{p_x\},$$ i.e., each line in the set corresponds to a pair $(u,p_y)$ for some $u\not=p_x$ such that $\beta(p_0,u,p_x)$. Similarly, the second set of lines is formed by connecting the point $p_x$ to each of the points in the set $$\{x\in P\mid \beta(p_0,x,p_y)\}\setminus\{p_y\}.$$
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: The domain is the set of intersection points of lines through $p_y$ and through $p_x$.

nodes.name: Domain and successor formulas
nodes.statement:
We then define the formulae  egin{align*} \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)\ := &\ \exists x y ig(P(x)\wedge P(y)\wedge eta^*(p_0,x,p_x)\wedge eta^*(p_0,y,p_y)\wedge eta^*(x,u,p_y)\wedge eta^*(y,u,p_x) ig)\ &\vee \Bigl(u
eq p_x\wedge u
eq p_y\wedge P(u)\wedge  igl( eta(p_0,u,p_x)\vee eta(p_0,u,p_y) igr) \Bigr),\ \varphi_{H}(u,v)\ :=&\ \exists x  igl( eta(p_0,x,p_y)\, \wedge\,  eta(x,u,v)\, \wedge\,  eta^*(u,v,p_x) igr) \wedge\,  orall r igl(\,  eta^*(u,r,v)\, ightarrow\, 
eg \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(r)\,  igr),\ \varphi_{V}(u,v)\ :=&\ \exists x  igl( eta(p_0,x,p_x)\, \wedge\,  eta(x,u,v)\, \wedge\,  eta^*(u,v,p_y) igr) \wedge\,  orall r igl(\,  eta^*(u,r,v)\, ightarrow\, 
eg \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(r)\,  igr). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define $\varphi_{Dom}$, $\varphi_H$, $\varphi_V$.

nodes.name: Diagonal formula
nodes.statement: Next we define the following auxiliary formula: \begin{align*} \mathit{diagonal}(u,v):=& \exists x\bigl( \varphi_\mathit{Dom}(x)\wedge \varphi_\mathit{H}(u,x)\wedge\varphi_\mathit{V}(x,v)\bigr). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define diagonal(u,v).

nodes.name: Tile formulas
nodes.statement: Recall the function $N$ that associates each tile type $t$ with the unique positive integer $N(t)$. Let $\exists^{=N(t)}x$ denote the quantifier stating that there exist exactly $N(t)$ $x$:s. Now, for each tile symbol $P_t$, we define \begin{align*} \varphi_{P_t}(u)\ :=&\ \exists z \exists^{=N(t)} x \bigl(\, \varphi_\mathit{Dom}(z)\wedge\mathit{diagonal}(u,z) \wedge P(x)\wedge \beta^*(u,x,z)\, \bigr). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define $\varphi_{P_t}$ by counting exactly $N(t)$ P-points on the diagonal.

nodes.name: Interpretation I
nodes.statement: The formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}$, $\varphi_\mathit{H}$, $\varphi_\mathit{V}$ and $\varphi_{P(t)}$ define the uniform interpretation $I$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: These formulas define the uniform interpretation $I$.

nodes.name: Interpreted structure
nodes.statement: Call $D_\mathfrak{C} := \{\ u\in T\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)\ \}$, and define the structure $$\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C} = (D_\mathfrak{C},H^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}},(P_t^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S}),$$ where \begin{align*} H^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}}\ :=&\ \{\ (u,v)\in D_\mathfrak{C}\times D_\mathfrak{C}\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_H(u,v)\ \}, \\ V^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}}\ :=&\ \{\ (u,v)\in D_\mathfrak{C}\times D_\mathfrak{C}\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_V(u,v)\ \},\\ P_t^{\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}}\ :=&\ \{\ u\in D_\mathfrak{C}\ |\ \mathfrak{C}\models\varphi_{P_t}(u)\ \}\text{ for each }P_t\in S. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define the structure $\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}$ cut out by the formulas.

nodes.name: Grid embeds
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{nonstandardmodelsexcluded}, it is easy to see that there is and $S$-labelled grid $(G,H,V,(P_t)_{P_t\in S})$ such that there exists an injection $f$ from the domain of the grid to $D_{\mathfrak{C}}$ such that the following three conditions hold for all $u,v\in G$ and $P_t\in S$: \begin{enumerate} \item $(u,v)\in H\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{H}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)$, \item $(u,v)\in V\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{V}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)$, \item $u\in P_{t}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{P_t}\bigl( f(u)\bigr)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: By the $\omega$-like sequence lemma an $S$-labelled grid injects into $D_\mathfrak{C}$.

nodes.name: Supergrid obtained
nodes.statement: Hence there is an $S$-labelled supergrid $\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}=(G_\mathfrak{C},H^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}},(P_t^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S})$ such that there exists a bijection $f$ from $G_\mathfrak{C}$ to $D_\mathfrak{C}$ such that the following conditions hold for all $u,v\in G_{\mathfrak{C}}$ and $P_t\in S$: \begin{enumerate} \item $(u,v)\in H^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{H}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)$, \item $(u,v)\in V^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{V}\bigl(f(u),f(v)\bigr)$, \item $u\in P^{\mathfrak{G}_\mathfrak{C}}_{t}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi_{P_t}\bigl( f(u)\bigr)$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\mathfrak{D}_\mathfrak{C}$ is isomorphic to an $S$-labelled supergrid.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Let $$\mathcal{G}(T,S):=\{\ \mathfrak{G}_{\mathfrak{C}}\in\mathcal{G}_S \ |\ \mathfrak{C}\in\mathcal{C}(T,S)\ \}.$$ Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $\mathfrak{G}_S\subseteq\mathcal{G}(T,S)$. The function $I$ is a uniform interpretation of $\mathcal{G}(T,S)$ in $\mathcal{C}(T,S)$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define $\mathcal{G}(T,S)$; linear extension in 2D gives $\mathfrak{G}_S\subseteq\mathcal{G}(T,S)$.

nodes.name: Vocabularies
nodes.statement: Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $n\geq 2$. Let $\sigma = \{H,V\}$ be the vocabulary of supergrids, and let $\tau = \{\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$ be the vocabulary of labelled Cartesian frames.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Note $n\geq 2$; fix the supergrid and Cartesian-frame vocabularies.

nodes.name: Frame sentence
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{boxedcartesianpicturesdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the tiling problem with a first-order $\tau$-sentence that defines the class of $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$. Let $\varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$ denote such a sentence.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Get $\varphi^S_{Cf}$ defining $S$-labelled Cartesian frames.

nodes.name: Tiling sentence
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the tiling problem with a first-order $\sigma\cup S$-sentence $\varphi_{S}$ such that a structure $\mathfrak{A}$ of the vocabulary $\sigma$ is $S$-tilable if and only if there is an expansion $\mathfrak{A}^*$ of the structure $\mathfrak{A}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{A}^*\models\varphi_{S}$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Get $\varphi_S$ expressing $S$-tilability.

nodes.name: Interpretation
nodes.statement: Now recall Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}. By Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}, since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, there exists a computable function $I$ such that for each input $S$ to the tiling problem, the function $I$ is a uniform interpretation of some class $\mathcal{G}(T,S)\supseteq \mathfrak{G}_S$ of $S$-labelled supergrids in the class $\mathcal{C}(T,S)$ of all $S$-labelled Cartesian frames with the domain $T$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Get the uniform interpretation $I$ of supergrids in Cartesian frames.

nodes.name: Reduction sentence
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an input to the tiling problem. Define the $\tau$-sentence \[ \psi_{S}\, :=\, \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S\, \wedge\, I(\, \varphi_{S}\, ). \]
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi_S=\varphi^S_{Cf}\wedge I(\varphi_S)$.

nodes.name: Equivalence to prove
nodes.statement: We will prove that for each input $S$ to the tiling problem, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There \emph{exists} an expansion $\mathfrak{B}$ of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\psi_S$. \item The grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: State the equivalence: $\psi_S$ satisfiable iff the grid is $S$-tilable.

nodes.name: Hardness from the reduction
nodes.statement: Thereby we establish that there exists a computable reduction from the \emph{complement problem} of the tiling problem to the membership problem of the first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$. Since the tiling problem is $\Pi_1^0$-complete, its complement problem is $\Sigma_1^0$-complete.\footnote{It is of course a well-known triviality that the complement $\overline{A}$ of a problem $A$ is $\Sigma^0_1$-hard if $A$ is $\Pi^0_1$-hard. Choose an arbitrary problem $B\in \Sigma^0_1$. Therefore $\overline{B}\in\Pi^0_1$. By the hardness of $A$, there is a computable reduction $f$ such that $x\in\overline{B}\Leftrightarrow f(x)\in A$, whence $x\in B\Leftrightarrow f(x)\in \overline{A}$.}
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: The equivalence reduces the $\Sigma^0_1$-complete complement of the tiling problem.

nodes.name: Tiling gives a model
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an input to the tiling problem. Assume first that the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable. Therefore there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{G}^*$ of the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ to the vocabulary $\{H,V\}\, \cup\, S$ such that $\mathfrak{G}^*\models\varphi_{S}$. Now since $\mathfrak{G}^*\in\mathfrak{G}_S\subseteq\mathcal{G}(T,S)$, by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} there exists an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ with the domain $T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models I(\varphi_{S})$. Since $\mathfrak{C}$ is an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame, we have $\mathfrak{C}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{C}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S\wedge I(\varphi_{S})$. Hence the Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ is an expansion of $(T,\beta)$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models\psi_S$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: From a tiling, Lemma on interpretations yields a frame satisfying $\psi_S$.

nodes.name: Model gives a tiling
nodes.statement: For the converse, assume that there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}$ of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$ such that we have $\mathfrak{B}\models\psi_S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{B}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$ and $\mathfrak{B}\models I(\varphi_{S})$. Since $\mathfrak{B}\models \varphi_{\mathit{Cf}}^S$, the structure $\mathfrak{B}$ is an $S$-labelled Cartesian frame with the domain $T$. Therefore, and since $\mathfrak{B}\models I(\varphi_{S})$, we conclude by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi_{S}$ for some $S$-labelled supergrid $\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{G}(T,S)$. Thus there exists a supergrid that is $S$-tilable. Hence the grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: From a model of $\psi_S$, an $S$-tilable supergrid and hence a tiled grid.

nodes.name: Condition 1
nodes.statement: There \emph{exists} an expansion $\mathfrak{B}$ of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\psi_S$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Some expansion of $(T,\beta)$ satisfies $\psi_S$.

nodes.name: Condition 2
nodes.statement: The grid $\mathfrak{G}$ is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: The grid is $S$-tilable.

nodes.name: Same as Sigma case
nodes.statement: The proof is essentially the same as the proof of Theorem \ref{infinitelemma}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Proof follows that of the $\Sigma^0_1$-hardness theorem.

nodes.name: Use recurrence grids
nodes.statement: The main difference is that we use Lemma \ref{recurrencegridinterpr} and interpret a class of labelled recurrence grids instead of a class of labelled supergrids, and hence obtain a reduction from the recurrent tiling problem instead of the ordinary tiling problem. Thereby we establish $\Pi^1_1$-hardness instead of $\Sigma_1^0$-hardness.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Interpret recurrence grids instead, reducing from the recurrent tiling problem.

nodes.name: Isomorphism essential
nodes.statement: Due to the recurrence condition of the recurrent tiling problem, the result of Lemma \ref{nonstandardmodelsexcluded} that there is an isomorphism from $(\mathbb{N},\mathit{succ})$ to $(P,E)$---rather than an embedding---is essential.
nodes.section: 4.2 Geometric structures with an undecidable unary expansion class
nodes.statement_short: Recurrence needs the isomorphism with $(\mathbb{N},succ)$, not just an embedding.

nodes.name: Fix S and frame
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of tile symbols. Let $\mathfrak{C}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ be an $S$-labelled $m\times k$ Cartesian frame.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Fix $S$ and an $S$-labelled $m\times k$ Cartesian frame.

nodes.name: Goal
nodes.statement: We shall show how to interpret an $S$-labelled $m\times k$ torus $\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}$ in $\mathfrak{C}$. The idea behind the interpretation is quite similar to the idea behind the interpretation in the proof of Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Interpret an $m\times k$ torus, as in the grid lemma.

nodes.name: Reuse grid formulas
nodes.statement: Recall the formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}$, $\varphi_{H}$, $\varphi_{V}$ and $\varphi_{P_t}$ defined in the proof of Lemma \ref{gridinterpretablelemma}. We shall now define variants of these formulae suitable for interpreting $S$-labelled tori in $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames. In the definitions of the new formulae, we shall make use of the old formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}$, $\varphi_{H}$, $\varphi_{V}$ and $\varphi_{P_t}$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Recall the grid formulas to be adapted.

nodes.name: Finite formulas
nodes.statement: We define \begin{align*} \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)&\ :=\ \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(u)\wedge \exists x\exists y\bigl(\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(x)\wedge \varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}(y)\wedge \varphi_H(u,x)\wedge \varphi_V(u,y) \bigr),\\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_H(u,v)&\ :=\ \varphi_H(u,v) \vee\Big(\beta(p_0,v,p_y)\wedge\beta(v,u,p_x)\wedge \forall x\big(\beta^*(u,x,p_x)\rightarrow\neg\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}^{\mathit{fin}}(x)\big)\Big),\\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_V(u,v)&\ :=\ \varphi_V(u,v) \vee\Big(\beta(p_0,v,p_x)\wedge\beta(v,u,p_y)\wedge \forall x\big(\beta^*(u,x,p_y)\rightarrow\neg\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}^{\mathit{fin}}(x)\big)\Big),\\ \varphi^\mathit{fin}_{P_t}(u)&\ :=\ \varphi_{P_t}(u)\text{ for each }P_t\in S. \end{align*}
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Define $\varphi^{fin}$ variants with wrap-around at the frame edges.

nodes.name: Interpreted structure
nodes.statement: Let $F_\mathfrak{C}:=\{u\in T \mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_{Dom}(u)\}$. Define the structure $$\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}=\bigl(F_\mathfrak{C},H^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}, (P_t^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S}\bigr),$$ where \begin{align*} H^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{(u,v)\in F_\mathfrak{C}\times F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_H(u,v)\}, \\ V^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{(u,v)\in F_\mathfrak{C}\times F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_V(u,v)\}, \\ P_t^{\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}}&:=\{u\in F_\mathfrak{C}\mid \mathfrak{C}\models \varphi^\mathit{fin}_{P_t}(u)\}, \end{align*} for all $P_t\in S$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Define the structure $\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}$.

nodes.name: Torus isomorphism
nodes.statement: It is straightforward to check that there exists an $S$-labelled $m\times k$ torus \[ \mathfrak{T}_{\mathfrak{C}}=\bigl(D,H^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}},V^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}}, (P_t^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}})_{P_t\in S}\bigr) \] and a bijection $f$ from $D$ to $F_\mathfrak{C}$ such that the following conditions hold for all $u,v\in D$. \begin{enumerate} \item $(u,v)\in H^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_H(f(u),f(v))$, \vspace{1pt} \item $(u,v)\in V^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi^{\mathit{fin}}_V(f(u),f(v))$, \vspace{1pt} \item $u\in P_t^{\mathfrak{T}_\mathfrak{C}}\ \Leftrightarrow\ \varphi^\mathit{fin}_{P_t}(f(u))$ for all $P_t\in S$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: $\mathfrak{F}_\mathfrak{C}$ is isomorphic to an $S$-labelled $m\times k$ torus.

nodes.name: All sizes realised
nodes.statement: Notice that since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, there exist $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames of all sizes $m\times k$ with all possible $S$-labelling configurations in the class $\mathcal{C}^{\mathit{fin}}(T,S)$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Linear extension in 2D gives frames of every size and labelling.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We have hence established that for all finite sets $S\not=\emptyset$ of tile symbols, the class of $S$-labelled tori is uniformly first-order interpretable in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$. Furthermore, the formulae $\varphi_{\mathit{Dom}}^\mathit{fin}$, $\varphi_H^\mathit{fin}$, $\varphi_V^\mathit{fin}$ and $\varphi_{P_t}^\mathit{fin}$ define the desired uniform interpretation $J$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: The formulas define the uniform interpretation $J$.

nodes.name: Vocabularies
nodes.statement: Since $T$ extends linearly in $\mathrm{2D}$, we have $n\geq 2$. Let $\sigma=\{H,V\}$ be the vocabulary of tori, and let $\tau=\{\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y\}$ be the vocabulary of labelled finite Cartesian frames.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Note $n\geq 2$; fix torus and finite-frame vocabularies.

nodes.name: Finite frame sentence
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{finitedefinable}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem with a first-order $\tau$-sentence that defines the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$ with respect to the class of all expansions of $(T,\beta)$ to the vocabulary $\tau$. Let $\varphi^S_{\mathit{fCf}}$ denote such a sentence.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Get $\varphi^S_{fCf}$ defining $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames.

nodes.name: Torus interpretation
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{torusinterpretablelemma}, there is a computable function $J$ such that for all inputs $S$ to the periodic tiling problem, the function $J$ is a uniform interpretation of the class of $S$-labelled tori in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with domain $T$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Get the uniform interpretation $J$ of tori.

nodes.name: Tiling sentence
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there is a computable function that associates each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem with a first-order $\sigma\cup S$-sentence $\varphi_S$ such that for all tori $\mathfrak{B}$, the torus $\mathfrak{B}$ is $S$-tilable iff there is an expansion $\mathfrak{B}^*$ of $\mathfrak{B}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{B}^*\models\varphi_{S}$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Get $\varphi_S$ expressing $S$-tilability of tori.

nodes.name: Reduction sentence
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be a finite nonempty set of tile symbols. Define the first-order $\tau$-sentence \[ \gamma_S:=\varphi_{\mathit{fCf}}^S\wedge J(\varphi_S). \]
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Define $\gamma_S=\varphi^S_{fCf}\wedge J(\varphi_S)$.

nodes.name: Equivalence to prove
nodes.statement: We will prove that for each input $S$ to the periodic tiling problem, the following conditions are equivalent. \begin{enumerate} \item There exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$. \item There exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: State: $\gamma_S$ satisfiable with finite $P$ iff some torus is $S$-tilable.

nodes.name: Hardness from the reduction
nodes.statement: Thereby we establish that there exists a computable reduction from the complement problem of the periodic tiling problem to the membership problem of the first-order theory of the unary expansion class of $(T,\beta)$ with a finite predicate. Since the periodic tiling problem is $\Sigma^0_1$-complete, its complement problem is $\Pi^0_1$-complete.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Reduces the $\Pi^0_1$-complete complement of the periodic tiling problem.

nodes.name: Tiling gives a model
nodes.statement: Let $S$ be an input to the periodic tiling problem. First assume that there exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable. Therefore, by Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma}, there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{T}^*$ of $\mathfrak{T}$ to the vocabulary $\sigma\cup S$ such that $\mathfrak{T}^*\models \varphi_S$. Since the function $J$ is a uniform interpretation of the class of $S$-labelled tori in the class of $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frames with the domain $T$, and since $\mathfrak{T}^*\models\varphi_S$, it follows by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that there exists an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ with the domain $T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models J(\varphi_S)$. Since $\mathfrak{C}$ is an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame, we have that $\mathfrak{C}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fcf}$. Therefore $\mathfrak{C}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fcf}\wedge J(\varphi_S)$. Hence the finite Cartesian frame $\mathfrak{C}$ is an expansion of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{C}\models\gamma_S$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: A tiled torus yields a finite frame satisfying $\gamma_S$.

nodes.name: Model gives a tiling
nodes.statement: For the converse, assume that there exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$. Therefore $\mathfrak{B}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fCf}$ and $\mathfrak{B}\models J_S(\varphi_S)$. Since $\mathfrak{B}\models\varphi^S_\mathit{fCf}$, the structure $\mathfrak{B}$ is an $S$-labelled finite Cartesian frame with domain $T$. Therefore, and since $\mathfrak{B}\models J(\varphi_S)$, we conclude by Lemma \ref{uniforminterpretationlemma} that $\mathfrak{A}\models\varphi_S$ holds for some $S$-labelled torus $\mathfrak{A}$. Hence by Lemma \ref{tilingdefinablelemma} there exists a torus that is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: A model of $\gamma_S$ yields an $S$-tilable torus.

nodes.name: Condition 1
nodes.statement: There exists an expansion $\mathfrak{B}=(T,\beta,P,p_0,p_x,p_y)$ of $(T,\beta)$ by a finite unary relation $P\subseteq T$ and constants $p_0,p_x,p_y\in T$ such that $\mathfrak{B}\models\gamma_S$.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Some finite expansion satisfies $\gamma_S$.

nodes.name: Condition 2
nodes.statement: There exists a torus $\mathfrak{T}$ such that $\mathfrak{T}$ is $S$-tilable.
nodes.section: 5 Geometric structures $(T,\beta)$ with an undecidable expansion class with a finite unary predicate
nodes.statement_short: Some torus is $S$-tilable.
